text:
Scrap the Parking Minimums

Most cities have a rule on their books that almost no resident has read and almost every resident pays for. It says that a new apartment must come with a set number of parking spaces, that a restaurant must provide a space for every few seats, that a bowling alley needs so many per lane. These minimum parking requirements were written decades ago, often copied from one city's code into another's, and they have shaped our streets more than any grand plan ever did. Cities should remove them.

Start with where the numbers come from. They are presented as engineering, but they are closer to folklore. The typical requirement is derived from surveys of peak demand at suburban sites with free parking and no public transport, then applied to every site in the city, including ones beside a train station. Nobody can explain why a funeral home needs exactly the number of spaces the code demands, because nobody ever worked it out. The planner Donald Shoup, who spent a career studying these rules, called them pseudoscience, and the description has held up.

The cost of this guesswork is large. A space in a surface lot costs thousands of dollars to build; a space in a structured or underground garage commonly costs tens of thousands. That money does not vanish. It is folded into rents, into the price of a meal, into the cost of groceries. A tenant who owns no car still pays for the stall under the building. A shopper who arrives by bus subsidises the driver parked outside. Because poorer households own fewer cars, the mandate works as a transfer from people with less to people with more, and it is invisible enough that hardly anyone objects.

The rules also stop housing from being built at all. On a small urban lot, the parking requirement is often the binding constraint: the land can fit the homes, or the spaces, but not both. The modest building types that used to fill out neighbourhoods, a few flats above a shop or a small block on a corner lot, become arithmetically impossible. Old buildings sit empty because a change of use would trigger a requirement that the site cannot physically meet. In cities short of housing, we are mandating storage for cars ahead of shelter for people.

Then there is what the mandates do to the place itself. Require enough parking everywhere and you get buildings set back behind asphalt, destinations too far apart to walk between, and bus services that cannot work because nothing is close to anything. Having made driving the only practical option, the city then observes that everyone drives and concludes the parking was needed. The requirement manufactures the demand it claims to measure. It also locks in more traffic, more emissions, more stormwater running off paved land, and more heat in summer.

The strongest objection is spillover. If a new building provides too little parking, residents will park on neighbouring streets, and the people already living there will bear the cost. This is a real concern, and it deserves a real answer rather than dismissal. But the answer is to manage the kerb, not to mandate the garage. Streets are public property, and cities have ordinary tools for rationing them: permits, time limits, meters priced to keep a few spaces free. Where on-street parking is managed properly, a developer who underbuilds has a product that is harder to sell, which is exactly the discipline we want. The mandate is a clumsy substitute for pricing something the city has been giving away.

It is worth being clear about what abolition does not do. It does not ban parking. Developers will still build it, because most buyers and tenants still want it, and lenders will still insist on it. What changes is who decides how much: the person risking money on the project, who has every reason to get it right, rather than a table in a zoning code. In places that have removed their mandates, among them Buffalo, Minneapolis and Austin, and across England since national policy shifted away from minimums, new buildings have kept including parking. They have included less of it where less was needed, and projects that were previously infeasible have gone ahead.

That evidence is not a promise of transformation. Removing parking minimums will not by itself fix housing costs or empty the roads, and anyone who says otherwise is overselling. Suburban sites will go on building large lots because their customers arrive by car. The reform matters most at the margin: the small infill site, the building near transit, the old shopfront waiting for a new use. But margins are where cities change.

The case comes down to a simple question. Should the law force every builder to provide a fixed amount of a costly thing, regardless of whether the people using the building want it? For almost any other product, we would find the idea strange. Parking deserves no exemption. Let people who want it pay for it, let people who do not go without, and let cities get back the land.
